source.title: Compute-Optimal Is Not Cluster-Optimal: Systems-Aware Scaling for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
source.authors: Soumajyoti Sarkar; Yuxin Tang; Sheng Zha

page_placements.theme: Hardware, storage and deployment costs change practical scaling optima

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper fits and validates a sparse-MoE training-loss scaling law, and reports that fitted coefficients vary with expert split factor and that compute-optimal allocations differ under model-FLOPs and hardware-deliverable budgets. It refines the scope of scaling-law and allocation claims rather than reproducing the original dense-model studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling-law fits, held-out-run losses, allocation sweeps, and staged pretraining results. The fitted target is smoothed final-checkpoint training loss, not held-out loss. The paper also discusses results from cited studies; those cited results are not cataloged here.
record.test_reason: The paper fits its own Chinchilla-style loss law to about 150 from-scratch sparse-MoE text-pretraining runs. It reports fit quality and held-out error on the largest runs, and shows coefficients drifting across expert split factor plus a ridge of unidentified coefficients. That is a new setting (sparse MoE) with results on V1, V2 and V7. Its allocation results (Figure 4, Section 7.4) are predictions derived from the fitted law and the authors' MOSAIC performance model, not measured tests of V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that staged runs reproduce the predicted MFU ordering and that loss ordering flips between model-FLOPs and hardware-compute axes. They say their evidence supports the hardware-aware ranking and co-design principle more than any single geometry, and that uncertainty in non-identified coefficients is not propagated.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sparse MoE language models and fits a four-dimensional training-loss law over total parameters, sparsity, tokens, and expert split factor, then couples it to a hardware performance model. It does not reproduce the original dense-model measurement and allocation recipes, and its fit target is training loss rather than held-out loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted coefficients vary across expert split factors; the selected architecture varies with cluster size and training window; the results are conditional on one geometry ladder, text-pretraining recipe, hardware platform, and Megatron-Core stack. The paper notes that the optimal G trend is not monotone.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the fitted law, model-FLOPs-optimal sparsity sits at the upper boundary of the data support. Under hardware-deliverable budgets (predicted MFU), the optimal sparsity is an interior plateau of about 0.915–0.963, and Nact* stays near 14–15B as the training window grows from 10 to 40 days.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For sparse MoE, the loss-optimal architecture depends on whether the budget is counted as model FLOPs or hardware-deliverable FLOPs (law- and performance-model-derived prediction).

fits_no_version.finding: In staged runs, the loss ordering of two MOSAIC-selected configurations flips between the model-FLOPs axis and the MFU-adjusted hardware-compute axis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ranking configurations by model FLOPs can misorder them relative to hardware cost.

record.problems: The fitted target is training rather than held-out loss. Several allocation recommendations extrapolate beyond the scaling-law training regime; the paper gives no empirical power-law exponents for optimal parameter and token counts versus compute. Many joint-law coefficients lie on a broad identifiability ridge, and that uncertainty is not propagated through the discrete search. Staged loss trajectories are presented in figures, and the conclusions are conditional on the selected geometry ladder, recipe, hardware, and systems stack.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows left out.

untested.parts: Dense models. Ranges beyond about 2.5 orders in Ntot and about 2.6 orders in compute (1.9e18–8.1e20).
Numerical loss prediction for runs orders of magnitude larger. The staged runs reach 15–20x the fit compute, but only the configuration ordering is reported, not predicted-vs-observed loss.
Entire version. No empirical power-law exponents for optimal N and D against compute. The Appendix D.3 allocation law is theoretical and conditional.
Entire version. Depth-to-width ratio is fixed by the geometry ladder.
Entire version. Text pretraining only, single pass.

missing.what: Joint-law coefficient identifiability: only beta (0.2070, CI 0.206–0.208) and eta (0.95) are identified. The rest, including alpha (0.1048), lie on a flat ridge; 400 fresh restarts show a wide near-flat ridge.
Asymptotic floor depends on sparsity: as Ntot and D go to infinity, loss approaches e + c(1-S)^-lambda, about 0.50 in the dense limit.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 exclusion on training-loss grounds is not followed: runs are single-pass, so final training loss is on unseen tokens, the same practice as Chinchilla. The V3 labels were removed because the allocation results are predictions from the authors' own framework, not measured compute-optimal exponents. Neither original source is the study.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits training loss, not held-out pretraining loss.

Held-out fits test the largest 10% of runs by active parameters within each expert-split-factor stratum, not numerical loss predictions at runs orders of magnitude larger. The staged runs extend beyond the fit range but are reported chiefly as ordering comparisons.

The paper does not empirically fit power-law exponents for optimal parameter count and token count against compute. Its discrete allocation sweeps are conditional on the stated geometry ladder, recipe, cluster, and hardware; the appendix's local allocation law requires assumptions about system-efficiency slopes.
No controlled comparison holds parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, and other architecture details.
The study is text pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The paper reports fit dependence across MoE expert-split factors and hardware settings, but does not compare alternative fitting methods on the same data or establish how exponents differ from the original dense-model studies.

tranche.reason: Beyond introducing a sparse-MoE setting, the study argues that allocation laws need systems-dependent qualification. Appendix D.3 derives power-law allocations only under approximately constant local MFU slopes; layout, memory and topology transitions change allocation phases. Sections 4.1 and B.2 also demonstrate coefficient dependence and non-identifiability.
